$comment: The performance budget, enforced by tools/perf-budget.mjs on every push.
docs/performance-budget.md explains where each number comes from and what
is and is not measured yet. Change a budget there and here together.

referenceMachine.label: mid-range laptop, 2026
referenceMachine.cpu: 4 physical cores, ~2.4 GHz sustained, no discrete GPU
referenceMachine.browser: current Chrome or Firefox, cold HTTP cache, warm DNS
referenceMachine.note: Deliberately not a developer machine. The atlas is for clinicians and students on institutional hardware.

comment: Byte budgets are converted to time with an explicit, stated model rather
than a hand-wave: one RTT to connect, one RTT per round of requests, then
bytes at the downlink rate. HTTP/2 over a static host serves the whole
critical path in one round of requests.
The model is pessimistic about bandwidth (no compression beyond gzip, no
CDN edge) and optimistic about nothing. It is a budget, not a prediction.

bundleGzipBytes.why: 150 KiB is the point at which a 25 Mbit/s link spends more time on our own code than on a round trip. Past that the page shell, not the network, is the thing to fix.

indexGzipBytes.why: The prebuilt indexes are on the critical path for first interaction, so they are capped well below the asset budget. 256 KiB holds the full ALC-1 level and frame tables with room for a label index per frame.

lowResAssetGzipBytes.covers: dist/assets/**, gzipped, excluding LICENSE and ATTRIBUTION.md
lowResAssetGzipBytes.why: 2.5 MiB at 25 Mbit/s is ~0.84 s of transfer, which fits the 2.5 s low-resolution asset budget with room for parse. It is also about the size a 20k-triangle body shell plus label sets lands at, so it constrains the asset pipeline without being unachievable.

indexParseMsNormalised.covers: JSON.parse of data/*.json plus building the lookup maps, normalised to the reference machine
indexParseMsNormalised.why: Main-thread work before the page can respond. 40 ms keeps it inside one frame budget's worth of slack on a 60 Hz display even after layout.

nameIndexBuildMsNormalised.covers: step 1 of app.js: assets/labels/names.json joined with coverings.json through joinNameIndex() and buildNameIndex(), which calls covering() once per structure, over the documents the build emitted. Found through the atlas index's own nameIndex descriptor, the way app.js finds it. Normalised to the reference machine.
nameIndexBuildMsNormalised.why: Boot-time main-thread work the page awaits before it can answer a click, so what it has to fit inside is FIRST INTERACTION and not one 60 Hz frame — nothing is painted yet, so no frame is being dropped. The ceiling is 5% of derivedFirstInteractionMs (5% of 3500 ms = 175 ms): the index may have a twentieth of the first-visit budget and no more, because the rest is transfer, parse and the viewer's first paint. Derived by DOG-98's rule, roundUpTo10(1.5 x this gate's own best-of-three reading), capped at that 175 ms. The reading is 64.2 ms, the highest of 22 runs of this gate on the branch this landed on: roundUpTo10(1.5 x 64.2 = 96.2) = 100, under the cap, so the cap does not bind. docs/performance-budget.md records the whole sample and the arithmetic. The 1.5x is for spread rather than slack — those 22 runs read between 26 ms and 64 ms, and almost all of that is the calibration's own noise, not the index's — because a limit set at the reading flaps red on a contended runner, which is how a line ends up switched off. The worst combination actually observed, the slowest build against the fastest calibration, is 77.8 ms: 78% of this limit. The figure gated here is a best-of-15, which is the machine's capability and not what a user pays; the cold first attempt runs about twice as long and is reported beside it, so this line and derivedFirstInteractionMs are both optimistic about this term by about that factor.

nameIndexBuildUsPerCell.covers: the same measurement as nameIndexBuildMsNormalised, divided by the number of cells the index binds (the sum of coverings[].cells, reported as nameIndex.cells)
nameIndexBuildUsPerCell.why: The invariant the absolute line cannot carry. Today's 57 structures and 3478 cells are the smallest index v1 will ever bind, so an absolute limit is consumed by growth and says less every time the atlas gets bigger, while a per-cell limit cannot be. It is also what stops DOG-80's quadratic covering() coming back: a quadratic prune reds this line at any scale, where the absolute line would only notice once the index was big enough. Derived by DOG-98's rule, roundUpTo2(1.5 x reading / cells), from the same 64.2 ms reading as the line above: roundUpTo2(1.5 x 64.2 / 3478 = 27.7 us) = 28. At today's 3478 cells that is 97.4 ms, marginally TIGHTER than the 100 ms absolute line, because the two roundings land differently — so at this scale a per-cell regression is what reds first, and the absolute line only leads once the index has grown. Over here means the cost of binding one cell moved, which is a real regression in covering() or the join; over on the absolute line alone means the index grew, and the gate says so itself.

lowResAssetParseMsNormalised.covers: JSON.parse of the low-resolution asset payloads, normalised to the reference machine
lowResAssetParseMsNormalised.why: Off the critical path for first interaction but on it for seeing anything. The viewer is expected to move this to a worker; until it does, 400 ms is the ceiling.

derivedLowResAssetLoadMs.covers: navigation start to low-resolution geometry parsed and ready, on the reference machine, derived from the byte and parse budgets through the transfer model
derivedLowResAssetLoadMs.why: The number a user feels. Under 2.5 s an atlas feels like a document; over it, like an application that is loading.

derivedFirstInteractionMs.covers: navigation start to the first click being handled, on the reference machine, derived as above plus a fixed render allowance
derivedFirstInteractionMs.why: Interaction is the product. 3.5 s is the outer edge of acceptable for a first visit to a 3D atlas, and the target to beat once the viewer lands.

renderAllowanceMs.comment: Fixed allowance for layout, first paint and the viewer's first GPU upload on the reference machine. A placeholder with a stated basis, not a measurement: it needs the viewer and a real browser to measure. Flagged as such in every report.

comment: CI runners are not mid-range laptops and their speed varies run to run,
so a raw parse time measured in CI cannot be compared to a budget stated
for a laptop. This fixed workload is run alongside the measurement and
used to normalise it:
normalised = measured * (referenceMs / observedCalibrationMs)
referenceMs is what the workload takes on the reference machine. It is a
single scalar and a crude one: it corrects for clock speed and little
else. Raw and normalised numbers are both always reported.
min/maxSpeedFactor bound where the correction is small enough to quote a
normalised number: past them the normalisation would be doing more work
than the measurement. Outside the band the gate does NOT quote one and
does NOT fail. It reports the unnormalised time as a one-sided bound —
a lower bound on a runner faster than the reference, an upper bound on a
slower one — and gates only in the direction that bound settles. Byte
budgets never touch the calibration and stay exact and hard either way.
Widening the band is not the way to make a fast runner green; it quotes
a bigger correction as if it were a measurement. The evidence that would
justify it is a measured distribution of this workload across the runner
pool, not a single reading. See docs/performance-budget.md.
